title: The financing regime of redistribution can reshape top-wealth accumulation and fiscal incidence
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35715; structurally estimated New Keynesian model with borrowers and savers, calibrated to U.S. macro-financial evidence
geography: United States; post-1980 fiscal-financing regime and top-income asset accumulation

observations.period: 1980s through 2026 paper; historical interpretation and model counterfactual

denominator.unit: U.S. structurally estimated macroeconomic model and historical fiscal-financing comparison

financing_regime_shift.value: redistributive policy financing shifted from inflationary finance toward debt finance backed by future taxation beginning in the early 1980s

top_wealth_response.value: under the model, funded transfers induce high-income households to accumulate claims on households and government

wealth_distribution_contribution.value: the shift from unfunded to funded redistribution contributed significantly to the subsequent saving glut of the rich

inflationary_finance_channel.value: unfunded transfers generate fiscal inflation that erodes the real value of public and private debt

observations.method: The authors develop a New Keynesian model with borrowers and savers, estimate it structurally, and compare funded transfers financed by future progressive taxation with unfunded transfers financed through inflationary erosion of debt.
observations.uncertainty: This is a model-based historical interpretation, not a direct household panel showing each transfer, tax payment, asset purchase, or welfare outcome. Results depend on the model structure, calibration, identification of the financing-regime shift, progressive-tax assumptions, and the treatment of inflation, debt, and asset markets. The record does not establish that top-wealth accumulation was caused only by fiscal financing or that a different regime would improve household welfare.
observations.subgroup: Borrowers, savers, high-income households, lower-income households, government, and private debt holders; the paper's macro groups are not a complete account of race, age, housing tenure, liquidity, business ownership, or household-level incidence.
observations.counterinterpretation: The saving glut may also reflect inequality, global safe-asset demand, demographics, technology, corporate behavior, housing, monetary policy, or other institutional changes. Debt finance can fund valuable public transfers, while inflationary finance can impose uneven costs; neither label alone identifies the better policy or actual distributional result.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI record for Working Paper 35715

boundary: This record adds a fiscal-financing-to-wealth-distribution mechanism. It does not directly observe a single household's transfer, tax, saving, debt, consumption, trust, political action, or durable security, and it does not rank inflationary versus debt finance as a universal welfare prescription.
